title: Buy Back an Hour Each Week
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that busy leaders should treat an hour of uncommitted personal time each week as something to be deliberately purchased back, not passively hoped for. It lays out three concrete mechanisms: paying for time-saving services (virtual assistants, delivery, landscaping), reducing friction through better systems (auto-pay, batched errands, standing grocery orders), and outsourcing low-judgment tasks entirely while retaining decision-making authority. The piece's underlying principle is a reframe of time-buying as investment rather than indulgence, arguing the value of the freed hour, used for strategic thinking, coaching, or family presence, typically exceeds the cost of the service that bought it back. It closes by contrasting a leader who spends the reclaimed hour on higher-value work or relationships with one who saves a small amount of money by personally waiting in a line, arguing the trade favors buying back time once a leader is honest about what their time is actually worth.
points: The piece's core reframe is treating an hour of personal time as something to buy back through spending, not something to find by working harder or faster.
It draws a specific line between delegating 'the mechanics of a task' and retaining 'the decisions,' offering leaders a boundary for what is safe to outsource versus what must stay with them.

It ties the value proposition explicitly to opportunity cost: the freed hour is worth more than its purchase price once spent on strategic thinking, coaching, or family presence rather than routine errands.
The comparison of 'buying back an hour' against 'saving fifteen dollars by waiting in line' operationalizes the argument into a concrete decision heuristic leaders can apply to everyday purchases.
The piece frames small friction-reducing systems (auto-pay, batched errands, standing delivery orders) as time savings 'hiding in plain sight' that require no ongoing spending decision once set up.
quotes: It's the hour you spend watching your child's soccer practice instead of catching up on emails in the parking lot, or the hour you use for a run instead of squeezing in one more call.
Once a leader is honest about the value of their time, gaining an hour is usually worth more than the cost of any service that buys that hour back.
Tasks that consume time without requiring judgment are ripe for delegation. As often as you can, delegate the mechanics of a task while keeping the decisions.
In fact, paying to have anything delivered that you usually wait in line for is a time saver hiding in plain sight.
An hour reclaimed each week is not an indulgence. It is an investment in the higher-value thinking, relationship building, and decision-making only a leader can do.

A leader who uses that hour to think strategically, coach a struggling team member, or simply be present with family members has made a better trade than someone who saved fifteen dollars by waiting in line for tickets.
